value: preference for nocturnal and early morning hours
method: 14 camera traps (Cuddeback Capture and Expert) in a grid, set 30 cm above ground, photographs only, 24 h, 30 s minimum delay; daily activity from a kernel density function fitted to bobcat records
conditions: Wild bobcats, Municipality of Cosoltepec, Mixteca region, Oaxaca, Mexico; December 2013 to September 2014, grid of 14 cameras covering 19.7 km2, 3,360 camera-trap days, data divided into four 60-day periods (two dry, two rainy). 32 photographic records, 28 independent events. Methods: 'According to the photographic records, bobcats were active day and night, so bobcat activity parameters over 24 hrs were used.' Results: two activity peaks, the first around 2:00 hrs and the second around 09:00 hrs; pattern similar between dry and rainy seasons, 'There was no statistically significant difference between seasons, possibly due to the small sample size (Wald test = 3.88; p-value = 0.050)'. Abstract: two peaks, 'one after midnight and the other after dawn, with very slight changes between seasons', and 'a preference for activity at night and early morning hours'. Discussion: the first peak began at night, peaked around midnight and decreased until sunrise; 'The second peak began mid-morning and decreased abruptly at noon', with low activity after noon; the authors relate night activity to temperature and to competition with gray fox, coyote and white-nosed coati. The Introduction (not the Discussion) says many authors report the species is cathemeral with activity peaks at crepuscule. The value is a stated preference, not exclusive activity: bobcats were recorded day and night. The paper's text mentions no bait, lure or attractant.

method: 61 camera traps (Bushnell Trophy Cam HD) at 40 cm above ground along natural trails; consecutive records of a species within 60 minutes counted as one independent event; daily activity pattern of pumas from independent records
conditions: Wild pumas in a forest remnant in the 3,986 ha Ucumari Natural Regional Park and the southern portion of the 21,131 ha Campoalegre Soil Conservation District, western slope of the Central Andes, Colombia; 61 cameras, four months in the dry season, December 2016 to March 2017, 3,070 trap-nights; 39 independent puma records. Cameras along natural trails at least 50 m from the main trails; 'no lures were used'. Results: onset of activity in late afternoon (17:00-18:00 h), peaking early in the night (20:00-22:00 h) and decreasing before sunrise (01:00-05:00 h); 'Subtle increases in puma activity were recorded during the day, especially at midday and early afternoon (12:00-13:00 h)'. Discussion: 'Puma activity patterns were mainly nocturnal in our study'; 'In view of the small sample size, the puma activity patterns we observed should be interpreted with caution.'; 'Furthermore, we were unable to discriminate between sexes in our records.' Only the dry season was sampled, so no seasonal comparison.

method: pairs of automated motion-triggered camera traps on trails and roads at 397 locations; honey badger daily activity pattern from photograph times and overlap with other carnivores
conditions: Wild honey badgers, Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve, Maharashtra, central India; dry-season survey February to June 2016; paired cameras at 397 locations on roads, animal trails and fire-lines, 30–40 cm above ground, stations active 26–30 days; 206 honey badger captures in 102 camera traps; the paper mentions no bait or lure. Results: 'Honey badgers showed an activity peak around midnight with <10% of the photographs between 0600 and 1,800 h.' Discussion: the nocturnal pattern 'was different from studies in Africa (Begg et al., 2016)'; African studies reported high temporal overlap with spotted hyaena and leopard, whereas here the badger avoided large carnivores, which the authors attribute to the different carnivore community. Caveats (printed): dry season only, monsoon sampling 'would reveal any differences in the activity pattern'; cameras sited on trails and roads for other carnivores, and the burrowing species would need a different detection strategy.
